name: Fairness Testing
description: Fairness testing checks whether a model treats otherwise identical inputs differently because of a protected attribute, by changing only that attribute, or a name, term or other proxy that signals it, and measuring how often or how much the output changes. In the form introduced by Galhotra, Brun and Meliou (2017), a tester generates inputs from a description of the valid input fields, makes copies of each that differ only in the protected attribute (for example, recorded sex), runs them all through the system as a black box, and reports the causal discrimination score: the share of inputs whose decision changes, sampled until it is known within a chosen margin of error and confidence level. For text, the same test substitutes identity terms or names in otherwise unchanged sentences, such as one religion or ethnicity for another, and reports the average change in the model's score across the substitutions, which Garg et al. (2019) call the counterfactual token fairness gap. Because every other part of the input is held fixed, the test needs no model of how the attribute influences other variables: it measures whether the system itself responds to the attribute, or to the chosen proxy, and the output is a score per attribute with the input pairs that failed.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team tests a credit-approval model before release. For a sample of last year's applications it changes only the applicant's recorded sex, and separately their marital status, re-scores each pair, and reports the share of decisions that flip with a confidence interval, against a release threshold agreed with the compliance function.

A trust-and-safety team checks a toxicity classifier used to hold comments for review by substituting identity terms such as 'gay', 'Muslim' or 'Black' across a set of non-toxic comments. It measures the average change in toxicity score for each term and flags any term whose substitution pushes benign comments over the moderation threshold.

An HR technology supplier tests its CV-ranking service before a client deploys it, by submitting the same CVs under first names and surnames associated with different ethnicities and genders and reporting how often each candidate's rank or shortlisting changes.

A hospital's AI assurance lead tests a symptom-triage assistant with clinical vignettes that differ only in the patient's stated ethnicity. Clinicians first mark which vignettes should be unaffected by ethnicity, and only those pairs count as failures when the urgency rating changes.

limitations.description: Holding every other input fixed measures only the system's direct response to the attribute or proxy. It does not follow through the effects the attribute has on other inputs, such as career breaks on an employment history, which Garg et al. note makes token substitution narrower than counterfactual fairness defined on a causal model. Where those downstream effects matter, a clean result does not show that individuals were treated fairly.

The test covers only what is perturbed. Discrimination through unlisted identity terms, unperturbed proxies, or references to a group that span several words goes undetected; Garg et al. found that mitigation which closed the gap for the listed terms generalised much less to held-out terms. A pass is a pass for the perturbations tried, and the list needs domain review.

Generated inputs may be unrealistic. Themis draws inputs uniformly from the input schema, so the score covers combinations that never occur in practice; restricting the test to real inputs or an existing test suite makes the score only as representative as that set, which Galhotra et al. note cannot be given a confidence level.

Not every substitution should leave the output unchanged. Garg et al. give 'That's so gay' versus 'That's so straight' as a pair a toxicity model may rightly score differently, and clinical risk can legitimately depend on sex. Without a judgement about which pairs must match, the test raises false alarms or, if such pairs are excluded wholesale, hides real failures.

A model can pass and still produce very different outcome or error rates across groups, because the test asks only whether changing the attribute changes the output, not whether outcomes are equal. Galhotra et al. distinguish this causal discrimination from group discrimination, and Garg et al. found that reducing the token fairness gap could worsen the true positive rate, so it does not replace group metrics.

resources.title: Fairness testing: testing software for discrimination
BiasFinder: Metamorphic Test Generation to Uncover Bias for Sentiment Analysis Systems
Counterfactual Fairness in Text Classification through Robustness
resources.abstract: In this paper, we study counterfactual fairness in text classification, which asks the question: How would the prediction change if the sensitive attribute referenced in the example were different? Toxicity classifiers demonstrate a counterfactual fairness issue by predicting that "Some people are gay" is toxic while "Some people are straight" is nontoxic. We offer a metric, counterfactual token fairness (CTF), for measuring this particular form of fairness in text classifiers, and describe its relationship with group fairness. Further, we offer three approaches, blindness, counterfactual augmentation, and counterfactual logit pairing (CLP), for optimizing counterfactual token fairness during training, bridging the robustness and fairness literature. Empirically, we find that blindness and CLP address counterfactual token fairness. The methods do not harm classifier performance, and have varying tradeoffs with group fairness. These approaches, both for measurement and optimization, provide a new path forward for addressing fairness concerns in text classification.

sample_claims.text: Changing only an applicant's recorded sex changes the credit model's decision for fewer than 0.5% of last year's applications, at 95% confidence.
Substituting any listed identity term into non-toxic comments changes the moderation classifier's toxicity score by less than 0.05 on average.
The CV-ranking service returns the same shortlist when names associated with different ethnicities and genders are swapped on otherwise identical CVs.
The triage assistant's urgency rating does not change when a patient's stated ethnicity is changed in vignettes that clinicians judged should be unaffected by it.
